questions.stem: In a patient diagnosed with Familial Dilated Cardiomyopathy (FDC), genetic studies reveal mutations in genes encoding proteins crucial for maintaining cardiac adherens junctions. Which specific protein alteration is most likely to contribute to the pathogenesis of FDC?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) β-Catenin

 

  • Familial Dilated Cardiomyopathy (FDC) can be associated with mutations in genes encoding for various proteins that are critical to the structure and function of the cardiac myocytes.
  • β-Catenin is a part of the cardiac adherens junctions, which are important for cell-cell adhesion and signalling among cardiac cells.
  • Mutations that affect these adherens junctions can compromise the integrity of the intercalated discs, leading to the weakening of the myocardial architecture seen in FDC.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. JAM-A (Junctional Adhesion Molecule-A): While JAM-A is involved in cell-cell adhesion, it is more relevant to tight junctions and leukocyte transmigration, not typically associated with cardiomyopathy.

 

Option B. Desmin: Desmin is an intermediate filament protein important for maintaining the integrity of the sarcomere in muscle cells. Mutations in desmin can lead to a form of cardiomyopathy, usually restrictive or arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, rather than FDC specifically.

 

Option D. Vimentin: Vimentin is also an intermediate filament protein, but it is not typically found in cardiac muscle cells; it is more associated with mesenchymal cells and not known to be a major factor in the pathogenesis of FDC.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • In the context of Familial Dilated Cardiomyopathy (FDC), mutations in genes encoding proteins that are part of the cardiac adherens junctions, such as β-catenin, can contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease by disrupting the structural integrity of the intercalated discs and myocardial architecture.

questions.stem: In a 45-year-old patient with a sudden-onset speech disorder, further investigations reveal a lesion in the left hemisphere involving the superior temporal gyrus and the posterior part of the left frontal lobe. The patient exhibits difficulty repeating spoken words without a corresponding impairment in language comprehension or production. Which intricate white matter tract is likely affected in this case?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Arcuate fasciculus

 

  • The arcuate fasciculus is a bundle of axons that forms part of the superior longitudinal fasciculus and connects Wernicke's area in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus with Broca's area in the posterior part of the frontal lobe.
  • Damage to this white matter tract can lead to conduction aphasia, which is characterized by the patient's difficulty in repeating spoken words while understanding and spontaneous speech remain relatively preserved.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Inferior occipitofrontal fasciculus: The inferior occipitofrontal fasciculus is a fiber tract that connects regions of the occipital lobe with the frontal areas. It is involved in visual processing and transmitting visual information to parts of the brain that are responsible for higher cognitive functions. Damage to this tract is not typically associated with isolated speech repetition difficulties.

 

Option C. Superior longitudinal fasciculus: The superior longitudinal fasciculus is a large bundle of fibers that runs along the entire length of the cerebral hemisphere, connecting the front of the brain with the back. It encompasses several subcomponents, including the arcuate fasciculus. While damage to the superior longitudinal fasciculus could affect a variety of cognitive and linguistic functions, it is the arcuate fasciculus specifically that is associated with the pattern of speech deficit described.

 

Option D. Anterior commissure: The anterior commissure is a bundle of fibers that connects the two cerebral hemispheres across the midline, primarily connecting temporal lobe structures. It is not primarily associated with language function but rather contributes to pain sensation and other interhemispheric communications. Damage to the anterior commissure would not typically result in the described speech disorder.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • In cases of sudden-onset speech disorders where the patient has difficulty with repetition but retains language comprehension and speech production, the arcuate fasciculus is the white matter tract likely to be affected.
  • This tract's role in connecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas is central to the process of repeating spoken language.

questions.stem: In a patient with chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, it is important to understand the role of specific stomach cells. Which factor is primarily associated with enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells of the stomach, and how does it contribute to the patient's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Histamine, which stimulates gastric acid production, potentially exacerbating ulcer symptoms.

options.label: B
options.text: Gastrin, which promotes mucus production and provides protection against ulcers.

options.label: C
options.text: Pepsinogen, an enzyme involved in protein digestion within the stomach.

options.label: D
options.text: Secretin, a hormone that regulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, influencing digestion.

questions.answerText: Histamine, which stimulates gastric acid production, potentially exacerbating ulcer symptoms.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Histamine, which stimulates gastric acid production, potentially exacerbating ulcer symptoms.

 

  • Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the stomach are primarily involved in the secretion of histamine, which plays a crucial role in regulating gastric acid secretion by parietal cells.
  • Histamine binds to H2 receptors on parietal cells, stimulating them to release more gastric acid. In conditions like chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, excessive or unregulated acid production can exacerbate ulcer symptoms by further damaging the gastric or duodenal mucosa.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Gastrin, which promotes mucus production and provides protection against ulcers: Gastrin is a hormone produced by G cells in the stomach, particularly in the antrum. It stimulates the secretion of gastric acid by parietal cells and promotes motility. Gastrin's role is not directly associated with ECL cells, but it can indirectly influence them by promoting histamine release, which then acts on parietal cells to increase acid secretion. However, gastrin itself does not promote mucus production for ulcer protection.

 

Option C. Pepsinogen, an enzyme involved in protein digestion within the stomach: Pepsinogen is secreted by chief cells in the stomach and is the precursor to the enzyme pepsin, which is activated by gastric acid. Pepsin plays a critical role in the initial digestion of proteins in the stomach. While important for digestive processes, pepsinogen is not associated with ECL cells nor does it directly contribute to the protective mechanisms against ulcers.

 

Option D. Secretin, a hormone that regulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, influencing digestion: Secretin is a hormone produced by S cells in the duodenum in response to acidic gastric contents entering the small intestine. It primarily functions to regulate the secretion of bicarbonate from the pancreas and bile ducts to neutralize stomach acid in the duodenum, protecting the intestinal lining and aiding in digestion. Secretin does not have a direct role in the stomach's function nor is it associated with ECL cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • In managing chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, the histamine from ECL cells helps in stimulating gastric acid production by aggravating ulcer symptoms and increasing mucosal damage.
  • Targeting this pathway with H2 receptor antagonists can be an effective strategy in reducing acid secretion and promoting ulcer healing.

questions.stem: Statement A: The migratory motor complex of the gastrointestinal tract will get repeated every 60 min Statement B: The migratory motor complex will be inactive during fasting periods Which one of the following statement is Accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The Statement A is True, the Statement B is False

options.label: B
options.text: The Statement A is False, the Statement B is True

options.label: C
options.text: Both the Statements A and B are True

options.label: D
options.text: Both the Statements A and B are False

questions.answerText: Both the Statements A and B are False
questions.solutionHtml:
US" style="font-size:14.0pt">Both the Statements A and B are False

 

Explanation:

 

  • The Migratory Motor Complex (MMC) or Migratory Myoelectric Complex will be active during the interdigestive periods and also during fasting
  • The Gastrointestinal Hormone Motilin (from M0 cells) will be involved in the initiation of migratory motor complex
  • These cycles of motor activity will migrate from the stomach to the distal ileum (in the aboral direction)
  • The entire cycle gets repeated every 90-100 min (not 60 min)

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The Migratory Motor Complex (MMC) typically occurs in cycles of about 90 to 120 minutes, not 60 minutes, and is active during fasting periods to clear the gastrointestinal tract of undigested material.

questions.stemHtml: A cardiologist is reviewing the electrocardiogram of a patient who is experiencing irregular heartbeats. They focus on the repolarization phase of the action potential. Which ionic movement is responsible for phase 3 of the cardiac action potential?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Potassium efflux 

 

  • During phase 3, increased permeability to potassium allows K+ to flow out of the cell, returning the membrane potential towards its resting level, a process essential for repolarization.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sodium influx: Incorrect. Sodium influx occurs during phase 0 of the action potential and is responsible for the rapid depolarization of the cardiac cell membrane.

 

Option C. Calcium influx: Incorrect. Calcium influx characterizes phase 2, the plateau phase, of the cardiac action potential, which sustains the depolarization and allows for the contraction of the heart muscle.

 

Option D. Sodium efflux: Incorrect. Sodium efflux is not a significant feature of phase 3; instead, the Na+/K+ ATPase helps restore the resting potential, but this occurs after repolarization.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The repolarization phase of the cardiac action potential, phase 3, is dominated by the efflux of potassium ions, which leads to the restoration of the resting membrane potential of cardiac muscle cells.

questions.stemHtml: While analyzing the impact of acute blood loss on cardiac function by interpreting changes in the Frank-Starling curves understanding how various clinical interventions or pathophysiological states affect stroke volume is vital. Given the patient's condition of mild hemorrhage and the associated compensatory mechanisms, to which point will the stroke volume shift from point X on the graph?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Point A

 

  • Mild hemorrhage leads to a reduction in preload due to blood loss.
  • The body compensates by increasing sympathetic activity, which enhances cardiac contractility and heart rate moves the stroke volume to a higher curve at Point A, maintaining cardiac output despite decreased venous return by increase in cardiac contractility.
  • So, the stroke volume (cardiac output) shifts to point A

 

 

 

Starling curve shifts up and to the left means increase in contractility & decrease in after load.

 

Down and right shifts mean decrease in contractility & increase in after load.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Point C: Incorrect. Point B suggests an increase in preload, which is not the case in hemorrhage; thus, it is not the appropriate shift following blood loss.

 

Option C. Point B: Incorrect. Point C indicates an excessive increase in contractility, which is beyond the typical compensatory response to mild hemorrhage and would not reflect the expected physiological change.

 

Option D. Point E: Incorrect. Point E implies decreased contractility, which contradicts the expected sympathetic response that increases contractility following mild hemorrhage.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Blood loss results in decreased preload and a subsequent shift to a lower stroke volume on the curve.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient presenting to the emergency department with sudden-onset of muscle spasms and tingling sensations and history of a recent thyroid surgery. The physician is alerted to the possibility of a rapid decrease in serum calcium levels. This sudden decrease in serum calcium is associated with:

options.label: C
options.text: Increased Sensitivity of Muscle and Nerve

questions.answerText: Increased Sensitivity of Muscle and Nerve
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>Sudden decrease in serum calcium is associated with increased sensitivity of muscle and nerve.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Increased Thyroxine and PTH: While thyroid and parathyroid hormones are critical in calcium metabolism, an increase in thyroxine and PTH would not directly cause the symptoms of hypocalcemia, such as muscle spasms and tingling sensations. These hormones typically act over a longer term to regulate calcium levels.

 

Option B. Increased Phosphate: Elevated phosphate levels can lead to decreased serum calcium due to the formation of calcium-phosphate products, but it does not directly cause the acute symptoms of hypocalcemia like increased muscle and nerve excitability.

 

Option D. Cardiac Conduction Abnormality: While hypocalcemia can affect cardiac conduction, presenting as an ECG change or arrhythmia, it is not the direct cause of muscle spasms and tingling sensations, which are more indicative of increased neuromuscular excitability due to low calcium levels.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • A sudden decrease in serum calcium primarily increases muscle and nerve sensitivity, leading to symptoms like spasms and tingling, and understand how this differs from effects on thyroid function, phosphate levels, and cardiac conduction.

questions.stem: A medical student is studying the mechanism of action of Vitamin D for a biochemistry exam. She is particularly interested in the characteristics of the Vitamin D receptor. Which of the following statements is true regarding the Vitamin D receptor?

options.label: A
options.text: Located on the Surface of the Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Dimerizes with Retinoid X Receptor.

 

  • The Vitamin D receptor (VDR) is an intracellular receptor that, upon binding with its ligand, the active form of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3), forms a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor (RXR).
  • This complex then binds to vitamin D response elements (VDREs) on the DNA, leading to the regulation of gene transcription.
  • This mechanism of action is critical for the biological functions of vitamin D, including calcium homeostasis and bone metabolism.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Located on the Surface of the Sarcoplasmic Reticulum: This is not accurate; the VDR is located  within the cytoplasm, not on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which is involved in muscle contraction.

 

 

Option C. Located on the Cell Membrane: VDR is an intracellular, not a membrane receptor. Membrane receptors typically act through second-messenger systems, whereas VDR functions directly as a transcription factor.

 

Option D. Dimerizes with PPAR-γ: VDR does not typically dimerize with PPAR-γ; it predominantly forms heterodimers with RXR.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Vitamin D receptor is an intracellular receptor that dimerizes with the Retinoid X Receptor to influence gene transcription.

questions.stem: Which of the following solutes is correctly paired with its exchangeability and contribution to osmotic activity?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Sodium - 65–70% exchangeable, osmotically active

 

  • Sodium ions in the body are about 65–70% exchangeable, meaning this fraction of the body’s sodium can be exchanged with sodium in the diet or excreted, which influences osmotic activity and therefore fluid balance.
  • This exchangeability and osmotic activity are crucial for maintaining proper fluid distribution and pressure within and outside cells.

 

Other Options:
 

Option B. Potassium - Mostly non-exchangeable, osmotically inactive: Incorrect because nearly all of the body's potassium is in the exchangeable pool and is osmotically active, significantly influencing cell function.

 

Option C. Calcium - Mostly exchangeable, osmotically active: Incorrect as almost all of the body’s calcium is non-exchangeable and primarily stored in bones and teeth, contributing minimally to osmotic pressure in fluids.

 

Option D. Magnesium - Mostly exchangeable, osmotically inactive: Incorrect because similar to calcium, a significant portion of the body’s magnesium is non-exchangeable, primarily stored in bones and involved in various enzymatic reactions rather than contributing to osmotic activity.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Sodium is 65–70% exchangeable and osmotically active, essential for fluid balance, whereas potassium is mostly exchangeable and also osmotically active, influencing cellular functions.
  • Conversely, the majority of calcium and magnesium in the body is non-exchangeable and does not contribute significantly to osmotic activity.

questions.stem: During a routine physiology lecture, a professor discusses the regulation of respiratory rhythm in humans. She explains the initiation of the RAMP signal. Which of the following regions in the brain is primarily responsible for initiating the RAMP signal?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Pre-Bötzinger complex

 

  • Pre-Bötzinger complex is critical for generating the respiratory rhythm and is particularly associated with the initiation of the RAMP signal during respiration.
  • The RAMP signal is a gradual increase in inspiratory drive that results in smooth, controlled inspiration.
  • The Pre-Bötzinger complex's role in this process is fundamental to normal breathing patterns, and it functions as the primary pacemaker for breathing.

 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Pneumotaxic centre: The Pneumotaxic centre is involved in regulating the rate and pattern of breathing but primarily acts to limit inspiration and promote a smoother transition between inhalation and exhalation. It does not initiate the RAMP signal.

 

Option C. Dorsal respiratory group (DRG): The Dorsal respiratory group (DRG) primarily processes sensory information and contributes to the regulation of breathing by influencing the depth and rate. However, it does not initiate the RAMP signal; instead, it responds to chemical and mechanical changes in the body.

 

Option D. Ventral respiratory group (VRG): The Ventral respiratory group (VRG) contains both inspiratory and expiratory neurons and is involved in generating the basic rhythm of breathing and active expiration, but it does not directly initiate the RAMP signal.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Pre-Bötzinger complex plays a central role in initiating the RAMP signal, crucial for generating a smooth and sustained inspiratory phase in respiratory rhythm.

questions.stem: In a discussion on neural pathways, a medical student asks about the transmission of dopamine from the substantia nigra. Which of the following areas receives dopamine via the efferent fiber bundle from the substantia nigra?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Corpus striatum

 

  • The substantia nigra, particularly its pars compacta segment, is a major source of dopaminergic neurons. These neurons project primarily to the corpus striatum (part of the basal ganglia) through the nigrostriatal pathway.
  • This pathway is essential for the modulation of movement, and its impairment is a key factor in Parkinson's disease, where there is a loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Tegmentum of pons: The tegmentum of pons does not receive a significant dopaminergic input from the substantia nigra.

 

Option B. Thalamus: The thalamus, although a crucial relay station for many neural pathways, does not directly receive dopaminergic fibers from the substantia nigra.

 

Option D. Tectum of midbrain: The tectum of the midbrain is involved in visual and auditory reflexes and does not receive direct dopaminergic projections from the substantia nigra.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The role of the substantia nigra's pars compacta helps in sending dopamine to the corpus striatum via the nigrostriatal pathway, a fundamental neuroanatomical feature crucial for the control of movement and affected in Parkinson's disease.

questions.stem: A surgeon is planning a vagotomy for a patient with peptic ulcer disease and discusses the potential impacts on gastrointestinal motor function. Which gastrointestinal motor activity is most likely to be affected by a vagotomy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Orad stomach accommodation

 

  • Vagotomy, which involves cutting the vagus nerve, significantly affects gastric functions that are modulated by vagal innervation.
  • Orad stomach accommodation refers to the stomach's ability to relax and expand in response to the entry of food, which is mediated by the vagus nerve.
  • This reflex allows the stomach to increase its volume without a corresponding rise in internal pressure, facilitating the initial stages of digestion.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Secondary esophageal peristalsis: Secondary esophageal peristalsis is initiated by distension of the esophagus rather than direct vagal control; thus it is less directly affected by a vagotomy.

 

Option C. Caudad stomach peristalsis: Caudad stomach peristalsis, which involves the peristaltic movements in the lower stomach responsible for grinding and propelling food into the duodenum, is influenced by the vagus nerve, but the primary impact of vagotomy is more pronounced on gastric accommodation.

 

Option D. Distension-induced intestinal segmentation: Distension-induced intestinal segmentation involves the local reflexes within the enteric nervous system for mixing food with digestive juices, and while the vagus nerve can modulate this activity, it is not as directly impacted by vagotomy as gastric accommodation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The critical takeaway is that orad stomach accommodation, which heavily relies on vagal innervation, is significantly affected by vagotomy.
  • This knowledge is important when considering the effects of surgical interventions on gastrointestinal function, particularly in patients with peptic ulcer disease.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old male undergoes surgery for carotid artery stenosis. During the procedure, the surgeon accidentally clamps the carotid artery just below the level of the carotid sinus. Which of the following physiological responses is most likely to occur due to this clamping?

options.label: A
options.text: Decreased heart rate and blood pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Increased activity of the vasomotor center

questions.answerText: Increased activity of the vasomotor center
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Increased activity of the vasomotor center

 

  • Clamping of the carotid artery below the carotid sinus reduces the blood flow and pressure detected by the baroreceptors located in the carotid sinus.
  • The baroreceptors, sensing a drop in pressure, decrease their firing rate.
  • This decrease in baroreceptor activity is interpreted by the vasomotor center in the brainstem as low blood pressure, leading to an increase in sympathetic outflow.
  • As a result, the vasomotor center increases its activity, which leads to vasoconstriction, increased heart rate, and elevated blood pressure in an attempt to restore perfusion.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Decreased heart rate and blood pressure: This is incorrect because a decrease in baroreceptor signaling due to reduced pressure in the carotid sinus would result in an increase in sympathetic nervous system activity, leading to increased heart rate and blood pressure, not a decrease.

 

Option B. Increased parasympathetic outflow: This is incorrect because the drop in baroreceptor signaling would lead to a decrease in parasympathetic activity and a compensatory increase in sympathetic activity to maintain blood pressure.

 

Option C. Decreased baroreceptor sensitivity: This is incorrect because the sensitivity of the baroreceptors themselves is not altered in this scenario. Rather, it is the reduced pressure sensed by them that results in decreased firing and subsequent physiological responses.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Clamping the carotid artery below the carotid sinus reduces pressure sensed by baroreceptors, leading to decreased afferent signaling, increased vasomotor center activity, and increased sympathetic response, resulting in elevated heart rate and blood pressure.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the sleep clinic with complaints of feeling unrefreshed after sleep and experiencing frequent awakenings. A polysomnography study is ordered, and the results show prominent features of sleep spindles and K-complexes. These findings are characteristic of which stage of sleep?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Stage 2 Non-REM sleep

 

  • Sleep spindles and K-complexes are characteristic features seen during Stage 2 of Non-REM sleep.
  • Sleep spindles are bursts of rapid, rhythmic brain wave activity, while K-complexes are sharp, high-amplitude waves followed by slower waves.
  • These features help in transitioning into deeper stages of sleep and play a role in memory consolidation.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. REM sleep: This is incorrect because REM sleep is characterized by rapid eye movements, low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG activity, and muscle atonia, not by sleep spindles and K-complexes.

 

Option B. Stage 1 Non-REM sleep: This is incorrect because Stage 1 Non-REM sleep is characterized by theta wave activity and is a lighter sleep stage. It lacks the distinctive sleep spindles and K-complexes seen in Stage 2.

 

Option D. Stage 3 Non-REM sleep: This is incorrect because Stage 3 Non-REM sleep, also known as deep sleep or slow-wave sleep, is marked by delta waves rather than sleep spindles and K-complexes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Sleep spindles and K-complexes are key features of Stage 2 Non-REM sleep and play a role in sleep stability and memory consolidation.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with a head injury following a fall. On examination, he is found to have elevated blood pressure, a heart rate of 45 beats per minute, and irregular breathing patterns. Which of the following reflexes is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Cushing's reflex

 

  • Cushing's reflex is a physiological response to increased intracranial pressure (ICP).
  •  It is characterized by the classic triad of hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration.
  • This reflex aims to maintain cerebral perfusion in the face of rising ICP by increasing systemic blood pressure.
  •  The bradycardia results from baroreceptor-mediated responses to the increased systemic pressure, and the irregular respiration is due to brainstem dysfunction caused by the elevated ICP.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bezold-Jarisch reflex: This reflex involves a decrease in heart rate and blood pressure triggered by stimulation of receptors in the heart, often seen in response to myocardial ischemia. It does not cause hypertension and irregular breathing patterns.

 

Option B. Hering-Breuer reflex: This reflex is involved in regulating the depth and frequency of breathing and is triggered by lung inflation. It is not associated with changes in blood pressure or bradycardia.

 

Option C. Bainbridge reflex: This reflex is triggered by increased venous return and results in an increase in heart rate to accommodate the greater blood volume. It is not related to the triad seen in Cushing's reflex.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Cushing's reflex is a critical response to elevated intracranial pressure, presenting with hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration.
  • Understanding this reflex is important for diagnosing conditions that increase intracranial pressure.

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old patient presents with symptoms of hyperparathyroidism. Laboratory analysis shows elevated levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH). The accompanying graph shows changes in plasma calcium and phosphate levels after administration of PTH. Which of the following mechanisms explains how PTH increases plasma calcium levels?

options.label: B
options.text: By promoting calcium absorption in the intestines

options.label: C
options.text: By increasing both osteoclastic activity and reducing renal calcium excretion

options.label: D
options.text: By enhancing phosphate absorption in the intestine

questions.answerText: By increasing both osteoclastic activity and reducing renal calcium excretion
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) By increasing both osteoclastic activity and reducing renal calcium excretion

 

  • Parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases blood calcium levels through two primary mechanisms:
    1. Increasing osteoclastic activity: PTH stimulates osteoclasts indirectly by acting on osteoblasts, which in turn produce signals that promote osteoclast activity. Osteoclasts break down bone, releasing calcium into the bloodstream.
    2. Decreasing renal calcium excretion: PTH acts on the kidneys to increase calcium reabsorption in the distal tubules, thus reducing the amount of calcium excreted in the urine.
  • Together, these actions lead to an increase in plasma calcium levels, as shown in the graph.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. By stimulating osteoblastic activity: Osteoblasts are involved in bone formation and would decrease plasma calcium by promoting its deposition into bone. PTH initially targets osteoblasts to indirectly stimulate osteoclasts, but its primary effect on blood calcium is through osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.

 

Option B. By promoting calcium absorption in the intestines: While PTH indirectly promotes intestinal calcium absorption through its role in stimulating vitamin D activation, this mechanism is not the primary way that PTH raises serum calcium acutely. Its more immediate effects are through bone resorption and renal calcium retention.

 

Option D. By enhancing phosphate absorption in the intestine: PTH actually decreases phosphate reabsorption in the kidneys, leading to increased phosphate excretion. This is the opposite of what would be expected if PTH enhanced phosphate absorption. Reducing serum phosphate indirectly helps increase calcium levels by reducing calcium-phosphate complex formation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases serum calcium levels primarily by stimulating osteoclasts to resorb bone and reducing renal calcium excretion, leading to increased blood calcium levels.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with a history of chronic acid reflux presents with worsening symptoms of peptic ulcer disease. Which type of gastric mucosal cells is primarily responsible for secreting a hormone that stimulates the production of hydrochloric acid in the stomach, potentially exacerbating his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) G cells

 

  • G cells are specialized cells located in the antrum of the stomach that secrete the hormone gastrin.
  •  Gastrin plays a crucial role in stimulating the parietal cells of the stomach to produce hydrochloric acid (HCl).
  •  Elevated levels of gastrin can increase acid secretion, which can exacerbate symptoms of acid reflux and peptic ulcer disease by increasing the acidity of the stomach environment.
  •  This makes G cells particularly relevant in conditions involving hyperacidity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Mo cells: Mo cells secrete motilin, a hormone that regulates gastrointestinal motility, not acid secretion. They are unrelated to the direct regulation of gastric acid production.

 

Option B. I cells: I cells are found in the duodenum and secrete cholecystokinin (CCK), which stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction. They do not have a role in the regulation of gastric acid secretion.

 

Option C. Peptic cells: Also known as chief cells, these secrete pepsinogen, an inactive enzyme that becomes pepsin in the presence of stomach acid. They are not involved in stimulating hydrochloric acid production.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • G cells in the stomach secrete gastrin, which stimulates parietal cells to produce hydrochloric acid (HCl), contributing to conditions like peptic ulcer disease and acid reflux by increasing gastric acidity.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of chronic heart failure is brought to the emergency department due to increasing shortness of breath, fatigue, and periods of rapid breathing followed by pauses in breathing during sleep. His wife reports that she has noticed these episodes of irregular breathing during the night, where his breathing pattern alternates between deep, rapid breaths and periods of no breathing. Physical examination reveals an elevated jugular venous pressure and bilateral crackles on lung auscultation. Which of the following best explains the underlying mechanism of this patient's breathing pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Hypersensitivity of the peripheral chemoreceptors to hypoxia

options.label: B
options.text: Increased respiratory drive due to metabolic acidosis

options.label: C
options.text: Delayed detection of changes in blood CO2 by central chemoreceptors

options.label: D
options.text: Increased lung stiffness leading to decreased tidal volume

questions.answerText: Delayed detection of changes in blood CO2 by central chemoreceptors
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Delayed detection of changes in blood CO2 by central chemoreceptors

 

  • Cheyne-Stokes breathing is a cyclic pattern of breathing characterized by periods of hyperventilation followed by apnea.
  • This abnormal respiratory pattern occurs due to a delayed response of the central chemoreceptors in detecting changes in arterial carbon dioxide (CO2) levels.
  • In patients with chronic heart failure, as seen in this case, reduced cardiac output leads to poor blood circulation, which in turn delays the transport of CO2 to the brain’s respiratory centers.
  • The central chemoreceptors, responsible for detecting CO2 levels, respond with a delay, causing alternating phases of hyperventilation (when CO2 is elevated) and apnea (when CO2 levels drop too low due to overcompensation).
  • The respiratory centers overshoot in response to these delayed signals, resulting in the waxing and waning pattern of breathing characteristic of Cheyne-Stokes respiration.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hypersensitivity of the peripheral chemoreceptors to hypoxia: Incorrect. While peripheral chemoreceptors respond to hypoxia, they are not primarily responsible for the cyclic breathing pattern seen in Cheyne-Stokes breathing. The main issue in Cheyne-Stokes is the delayed feedback in response to changes in blood CO2 levels, which does not involve hypoxia sensitivity as the primary cause.

 

Option B. Increased respiratory drive due to metabolic acidosis: Incorrect. Metabolic acidosis increases the respiratory drive and can lead to rapid, deep breathing (Kussmaul breathing), not the cyclical waxing and waning pattern characteristic of Cheyne-Stokes breathing.

 

Option D. Increased lung stiffness leading to decreased tidal volume: Incorrect. Increased lung stiffness (as seen in conditions like pulmonary fibrosis) may result in shallow, rapid breathing, but it does not lead to the cyclical breathing pattern of hyperventilation followed by apnea that defines Cheyne-Stokes breathing.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Cheyne-Stokes breathing is characterized by alternating periods of hyperventilation and apnea.
  • It occurs due to delayed detection of blood CO2 changes by central chemoreceptors, often seen in patients with heart failure or neurological damage.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man visits the clinic for a routine checkup. During the neurological examination, you assess his sensory perception. The patient is able to sense skin stretching and responds appropriately to joint position changes. These sensory modalities are primarily mediated by mechanoreceptors located in the skin and joints. Which of the following mechanoreceptors is most likely responsible for detecting skin stretch and contributing to joint position sense in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Ruffini corpuscles

 

  • Ruffini corpuscles are slowly adapting mechanoreceptors found in the skin and joints.
  • They are specialized for detecting skin stretch and are involved in providing information related to joint position and movement.
  • Ruffini corpuscles play a critical role in proprioception, helping the body understand limb positioning and the movement of joints, as well as the stretching of skin during movement.
  • This allows the patient to accurately perceive changes in skin tension and the position of their joints, as described in this clinical case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pacinian corpuscles: Incorrect. Pacinian corpuscles are mechanoreceptors that detect deep pressure and vibration, not skin stretch or joint position sense. They are rapidly adapting and respond to transient mechanical changes rather than continuous skin stretch or proprioceptive input.

 

Option B. Meissner corpuscles: Incorrect. Meissner corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors responsible for detecting light touch and fine tactile discrimination, especially in areas like the fingertips. They do not detect skin stretch or provide information about joint position.

 

Option D. Merkel cells: Incorrect. Merkel cells are mechanoreceptors that detect sustained pressure and texture, helping in fine tactile sensing such as detecting textures and shapes. However, they are not involved in sensing skin stretch or joint position.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Ruffini corpuscles are mechanoreceptors responsible for detecting skin stretch and providing information about joint position and movement, playing an essential role in proprioception.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best explains the rise in blood pressure during the early phase of the Valsalva maneuver?

options.label: C
options.text: Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to left ventricular pressure

questions.answerText: Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure

 

  • The Valsalva maneuver consists of forced expiration against a closed glottis, which increases intrathoracic pressure.
  • During Phase I of the maneuver, the rise in intrathoracic pressure is transmitted to the aorta, resulting in a transient increase in blood pressure.
  • This occurs because the elevated pressure in the thoracic cavity temporarily compresses the aorta, leading to an increase in aortic pressure before the blood flow begins to decrease due to reduced venous return.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increase in left atrial pressure: Incorrect. While intrathoracic pressure increases left atrial pressure during the Valsalva maneuver, this does not directly cause the rise in blood pressure observed during Phase I. The pressure rise is primarily due to increased aortic pressure.

 

Option B. Increase in left ventricular volume: Incorrect. Left ventricular volume does not increase during the initial phase of the Valsalva maneuver. In fact, as intrathoracic pressure increases, venous return to the heart decreases, leading to a subsequent decrease in left ventricular filling during later phases.

 

Option D. Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to left ventricular pressure: Incorrect. Although intrathoracic pressure increases during the Valsalva maneuver, the immediate rise in blood pressure is due to the increase in aortic pressure rather than left ventricular pressure.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • During Phase I of the Valsalva maneuver, the increase in intrathoracic pressure is transmitted to the aorta, resulting in a transient rise in aortic pressure and blood pressure.
  • This precedes the drop in venous return that characterizes later phases of the maneuver.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following conditions is most likely associated with the leftward shift of the pressure-volume loop?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Aortic stenosis

 

  • A leftward shift of the pressure-volume loop indicates that the heart is working at a lower end-diastolic volume and higher pressures, consistent with aortic stenosis.
  • In aortic stenosis, the left ventricle must generate significantly higher pressures to overcome the narrowed aortic valve, resulting in a taller and narrower loop.
  • The ventricle's ability to fill may also be reduced, leading to a smaller end-diastolic volume, causing the loop to shift leftward.
  • The narrowed aortic valve increases afterload, which is the hallmark of aortic stenosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Aortic regurgitation: Incorrect. Aortic regurgitation results in an increase in left ventricular volume due to the backflow of blood into the ventricle during diastole, leading to a rightward and widened loop, not a leftward shift. The loop also shows increased stroke volume due to the extra volume regurgitated back into the ventricle.

 

Option B. Mitral regurgitation: Incorrect. Mitral regurgitation is characterized by an increase in left ventricular volume due to backflow of blood from the ventricle into the left atrium during systole, causing a rightward shift in the loop. The loop becomes wider due to the increased volume in the ventricle, but there is no leftward shift.

 

Option D. Congestive cardiac failure: Incorrect. Congestive cardiac failure typically leads to a downward and rightward shift of the loop due to reduced contractility and higher end-diastolic volumes, not a leftward shift. The loop reflects impaired systolic function and reduced ejection fraction.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • A leftward shift of the pressure-volume loop is indicative of aortic stenosis, where the heart generates higher pressures at lower volumes due to increased afterload from the stenotic aortic valve.
  • The ventricle must work harder to pump blood through the narrowed valve, leading to this characteristic change in the loop.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old male chronic alcoholic is admitted to the general medicine ward with symptoms of abdominal distention, yellowish discoloration of the eyes, and abdominal pain. He is diagnosed with decompensated liver disease. All of the following clotting factors will be affected in this patient except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Factor VIII

 

  • In decompensated liver disease, the synthesis of most clotting factors is impaired due to the liver's compromised function. The liver produces several clotting factors, including Factors II, VII, and IX, which are vitamin K-dependent.
  • However, Factor VIII is synthesized by endothelial cells, primarily in the liver but also in other tissues, and its levels can actually be normal or elevated in liver disease due to decreased clearance.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Factor II: Factor II (prothrombin) is produced in the liver and is dependent on vitamin K for its synthesis. It is typically reduced in liver disease.

 

Option B. Factor VII: Factor VII is another vitamin K-dependent clotting factor synthesized by the liver and is commonly reduced in liver disease.

 

Option D. Factor IX: Factor IX is also synthesized in the liver and is dependent on vitamin K. It is typically reduced in liver disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • In decompensated liver disease, the synthesis of most clotting factors, including Factors II, VII, and IX, is impaired due to the liver's compromised function.
  • Factor VIII, however, is less affected because it is primarily produced by endothelial cells, not hepatocytes, and may remain normal or even elevated.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of chronic heart failure is undergoing evaluation for his condition. During an arterial pulse waveform analysis, the presence of a dicrotic notch is noted. The dicrotic notch in the arterial pulse waveform corresponds to which of the following events?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Closure of aortic valve

 

  • The dicrotic notch in the arterial pulse waveform represents the closure of the aortic valve.
  • When the left ventricle finishes ejecting blood into the aorta, the aortic valve closes to prevent backflow into the ventricle.
  • This closure causes a brief and characteristic dip in the arterial pressure waveform, known as the dicrotic notch, marking the end of systole and the beginning of diastole.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Opening of mitral valve: The opening of the mitral valve occurs during diastole, allowing blood to flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle. This event does not produce a dicrotic notch in the arterial pulse waveform.

 

Option B. Closure of mitral valve: The closure of the mitral valve marks the beginning of ventricular systole, which prevents blood from flowing back into the left atrium. This event is associated with the first heart sound (S1) but does not produce a dicrotic notch in the arterial pulse waveform.

 

Option C. Opening of aortic valve: The opening of the aortic valve occurs at the start of systole, allowing the left ventricle to eject blood into the aorta. This event does not create a dicrotic notch in the arterial pulse waveform.

 

Educational objective:

 

  • The dicrotic notch in the arterial pulse waveform is associated with the closure of the aortic valve, signaling the end of systole and the beginning of diastole.

questions.stemHtml: A respiratory physiology seminar presents a pressure-volume loop obtained from a patient during mechanical ventilation. The difference in the course of the inspiratory loop and the expiratory loop in the curve is being discussed. The difference in the course of the inspiratory loop and the expiratory loop in the curve is due to which of the following conditions:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Difference in Surfactant Concentration

 

  • The pressure-volume loop shown in the image displays hysteresis, which is the difference between the inflation (inspiration) and deflation (expiration) curves.
  • This hysteresis is primarily due to the dynamic properties of the lung's surfactant, which reduces surface tension and thereby influences lung compliance differently during inflation and deflation.
  • During inspiration, the surfactant molecules are more spread out, resulting in higher surface tension and lower compliance. During expiration, the surfactant molecules become more concentrated, decreasing surface tension and increasing compliance.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Difference in Alveolar Pressure: While alveolar pressure changes during breathing, the primary cause of the hysteresis observed in the pressure-volume loop is related to surfactant dynamics rather than direct changes in alveolar pressure.

 

Option C. Difference in Airway Resistance: Airway resistance affects the flow of air but does not significantly contribute to the hysteresis seen in the pressure-volume loop. The loop's shape is more influenced by lung compliance and surfactant properties.

 

Option D. Active Inspiration, Passive Expiration: Although inspiration is typically an active process and expiration is usually passive, this does not explain the hysteresis in the pressure-volume loop. The hysteresis is due to the properties of the lung tissue and surfactant rather than the muscular activity involved in breathing.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The difference in the course of the inspiratory and expiratory loops in the pressure-volume curve (hysteresis) is primarily due to the difference in surfactant concentration, which affects lung compliance during inflation and deflation.

questions.stem: During a ward round, a 42-year-old patient is being discussed due to concerns about dehydration and electrolyte imbalance. The professor explains the role of the countercurrent system in the kidneys in maintaining water and solute balance to the medical interns. Which of the following will function as the countercurrent exchanger in the countercurrent system of the kidneys?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Vasa Recta

 

  • The vasa recta are a series of straight capillaries in the medulla of the kidney that lie parallel to the loop of Henle.
  • They function as the counter current exchangers in the kidney's counter current system.
  • The vasa recta play a crucial role in maintaining the osmotic gradient in the renal medulla, which is essential for the concentration of urine.
  • They achieve this by allowing blood to flow slowly and in a counter current direction relative to the flow of filtrate in the loop of Henle, thus facilitating the exchange of solutes and water without dissipating the osmotic gradient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Peritubular Capillaries: Peritubular capillaries surround the proximal and distal tubules and are involved in the reabsorption of solutes and water, but they do not function as the counter current exchangers.

 

Option B. Loop of Henle: The loop of Henle functions as the counter current multiplier, which helps establish the osmotic gradient in the renal medulla. However, it is not the exchanger; it multiplies the concentration gradient.

 

Option D. Juxtaglomerular Apparatus: The juxtaglomerular apparatus is involved in regulating blood pressure and the filtration rate of the glomerulus through the release of renin, but it is not involved in the counter current exchange process.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The vasa recta function as the counter current exchangers in the kidneys, maintaining the osmotic gradient necessary for the concentration of urine and the regulation of water and solute balance.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents with symptoms of malabsorption. In the process of fat digestion and absorption, which sequence correctly outlines the activation of various lipases in the gastrointestinal tract?

options.label: A
options.text: Pancreatic Lipase, Lingual Lipase, Gastric Lipase

options.label: B
options.text: Lingual Lipase, Gastric Lipase, Pancreatic Lipase

options.label: C
options.text: Gastric Lipase, Lingual Lipase, Pancreatic Lipase

options.label: D
options.text: Pancreatic Lipase, Gastric Lipase, Lingual Lipase

questions.answerText: Lingual Lipase, Gastric Lipase, Pancreatic Lipase
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lingual Lipase, Gastric Lipase, Pancreatic Lipase

 

  • The correct sequence of lipase activation in the gastrointestinal tract begins with lingual lipase, followed by gastric lipase, and then pancreatic lipase.
  • Lingual Lipase: Secreted by the glands in the tongue, lingual lipase begins the digestion of fats in the mouth, particularly effective in breaking down short- and medium-chain fatty acids.
  • Gastric Lipase: Produced by the stomach, gastric lipase continues the digestion of fats, particularly in the acidic environment of the stomach, further breaking down triglycerides into diglycerides and free fatty acids.
  • Pancreatic Lipase: Secreted by the pancreas into the small intestine, pancreatic lipase is the primary enzyme for fat digestion, breaking down triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids in the alkaline environment of the small intestine.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The correct sequence of lipase activation in the gastrointestinal tract is lingual lipase, gastric lipase, and then pancreatic lipase, each playing a specific role in the digestion of dietary fats.

questions.stem: A patient is experiencing gastrointestinal motility issues, specifically involving anterograde dilatation of the small intestine. Which neurotransmitter is responsible for this physiological action?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) VIP

 

  • Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) is the neurotransmitter responsible for anterograde dilatation of the small intestine.
  • VIP is a neuropeptide that acts as a potent vasodilator and relaxes smooth muscles in the gastrointestinal tract.
  • It promotes intestinal motility by inducing smooth muscle relaxation, increasing water and electrolyte secretion, and dilating blood vessels, thus facilitating the anterograde movement of intestinal contents.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Acetylcholine: Acetylcholine primarily acts as a neurotransmitter that stimulates smooth muscle contraction in the gastrointestinal tract, promoting motility rather than causing dilatation.

 

Option B. Serotonin: Serotonin (5-HT) mainly acts to enhance gut motility by stimulating smooth muscle contraction and coordinating peristalsis but is not directly responsible for anterograde dilatation.

 

Option D. Substance P: Substance P is a neuropeptide involved in pain transmission and can also stimulate smooth muscle contraction in the gastrointestinal tract, but it does not induce dilatation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) is the neurotransmitter that causes anterograde dilatation of the small intestine by promoting smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation.

questions.stemHtml: In a patient, the hypothalamic thermostat was reset from point V to point X on the graph. Which of the following happens in stage W compared to stage Y?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Shivering

 

  • In the context of thermoregulation, stage W corresponds to the phase where the body temperature is rising to meet the new hypothalamic set point (from V to X), while stage Y corresponds to the phase where the body temperature is falling back to the original set point (from X to Z).
  • During stage W, mechanisms that generate heat, such as shivering, are activated to raise the body temperature to the new set point.
  • In contrast, during stage Y, the body activates mechanisms to dissipate heat, such as sweating and increased blood flow to the skin, to lower the temperature.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sweating: Sweating occurs during stage Y when the body is attempting to lower its temperature after the set point has been reset to normal.

 

Option C. Increased blood flow to skin: This also happens during stage Y to help dissipate heat and lower body temperature.

 

Option D. Inhibition of chemical thermogenesis: This occurs during stage Y to reduce heat production as the body cools down.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • During stage W, when the body is raising its temperature to match a new set point, shivering is the primary mechanism activated to generate heat.

questions.stem: A patient with iron deficiency anemia is being evaluated for proper iron absorption in the gastrointestinal tract. Which of the following is the transporter responsible for iron uptake into enterocytes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Divalent Metal Transporter 1

 

  • Divalent Metal Transporter 1 (DMT1) is the primary transporter responsible for the uptake of ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) into enterocytes in the duodenum.
  • DMT1 facilitates the transport of iron across the apical membrane of the enterocyte, allowing it to enter the cell from the intestinal lumen.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ferroportin 1: This transporter is responsible for exporting iron from enterocytes into the bloodstream across the basolateral membrane, not for uptake into enterocytes.

 

Option B. Hephaestin: This protein works in conjunction with ferroportin to oxidize ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) to ferric iron (Fe³⁺) as it is transported out of enterocytes into the bloodstream.

 

Option D. Divalent Metal Transporter 2: There is no known DMT2; DMT1 is the known transporter for divalent metal ions, including iron.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Divalent Metal Transporter 1 (DMT1) is the key transporter responsible for the uptake of iron into enterocytes from the intestinal lumen.

questions.stem: Consider the following statements regarding cardiac pacemaker cells: Statement A: The f channels are seen in cardiac pacemaker cells. Statement B: The f channels are activated following depolarization, resulting in the action potential. Which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The statement A is true, the statement B is false

options.label: B
options.text: The statement A is false, the statement B is true

options.label: C
options.text: Both the statements A and B are true

options.label: D
options.text: Both the statements A and B are false

questions.answerText: The statement A is true, the statement B is false
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) The statement A is true, the statement B is false

 

Statement A: The f channels, also known as funny channels or HCN channels (hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channels), are indeed present in cardiac pacemaker cells. These channels play a crucial role in the pacemaker potential that controls the rhythmic heartbeat.

 

Statement B: The f channels are activated by hyperpolarization, not depolarization. When the membrane potential becomes more negative (hyperpolarizes), these channels open, allowing an influx of sodium ions (and some potassium ions) which leads to a gradual depolarization. This slow depolarization helps to bring the membrane potential to the threshold needed to trigger the next action potential. Therefore, statement B is false.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The f channels (funny channels) are present in cardiac pacemaker cells and are activated by hyperpolarization, not depolarization.
  • They play a key role in initiating the pacemaker potential that leads to the rhythmic generation of action potentials in the heart.


ore, statement B is false.

questions.stem: Which of the following hormones uses receptor tyrosine kinase signaling?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Insulin

 

  • Insulin uses receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling.
  • When insulin binds to its receptor, which is a receptor tyrosine kinase, it induces autophosphorylation of the receptor and subsequent phosphorylation of intracellular substrates.
  • This cascade of events leads to various metabolic effects, including increased glucose uptake by cells, glycogen synthesis, and lipid metabolism.
  • The RTK pathway is crucial for mediating the effects of insulin on glucose homeostasis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. TSH (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone): TSH uses the G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling pathway, specifically the adenylate cyclase-cAMP pathway, to exert its effects on the thyroid gland, stimulating the production of thyroid hormones.

 

Option B. MSH (Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone): MSH also utilizes the G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling pathway, specifically the cAMP pathway, to influence melanocytes and affect pigmentation.

 

Option C. TRH (Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone): TRH acts through G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) that activate phospholipase C, leading to the production of inositol triphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG), which increase intracellular calcium levels.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Insulin uses receptor tyrosine kinase signaling to exert its metabolic effects, including glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis.
  • This pathway is distinct from the G-protein coupled receptor pathways used by hormones like TSH, MSH, and TRH.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with a vascular injury affecting the inferior frontal gyrus. Which functional area is likely to be impacted?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Motor speech area

 

  • The inferior frontal gyrus is part of the frontal lobe of the brain and includes Broca's area, which is the motor speech area.
  • Broca's area is responsible for language production and articulation.
  • Damage to this area can result in Broca's aphasia, characterized by difficulties in speech production while comprehension generally remains intact.
  • This area is crucial for the motor aspects of speech, such as forming words and constructing sentences.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Auditory area: The auditory area, also known as the primary auditory cortex, is located in the temporal lobe. It is responsible for processing auditory information and is not located in the inferior frontal gyrus.

 

Option C. Visual area: The visual area, also known as the primary visual cortex, is located in the occipital lobe. It is responsible for processing visual information and is not affected by damage to the inferior frontal gyrus.

 

Option D. Wernicke's area: Wernicke's area is involved in language comprehension and is located in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus. It is not located in the inferior frontal gyrus, so damage to this area does not affect Wernicke's area.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The motor speech area, or Broca's area, is located in the inferior frontal gyrus and is responsible for language production and articulation.
  • Damage to this area can lead to Broca's aphasia, characterized by impaired speech production.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient is being evaluated for his body's response to low oxygen levels. Which of the following ions is involved in the mechanism of peripheral oxygen sensing by chemoreceptors?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Potassium

 

  • Potassium ions play a crucial role in the mechanism of peripheral oxygen sensing by chemoreceptors, particularly in the carotid bodies.
  • When oxygen levels drop, the activity of oxygen-sensitive potassium channels in the cell membranes of the chemoreceptors decreases.
  • This reduction in potassium efflux leads to cell depolarization, which subsequently opens voltage-gated calcium channels, resulting in an influx of calcium.
  • The increased intracellular calcium concentration triggers neurotransmitter release, which signals the respiratory centers in the brain to increase ventilation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sodium: While sodium ions are essential in various physiological processes, they are not primarily involved in the specific mechanism of peripheral oxygen sensing by chemoreceptors.

 

Option B. Calcium: Calcium ions are involved in the downstream effects following the initial sensing of low oxygen by potassium channels. They enter the cells following depolarization, leading to neurotransmitter release, but they are not the primary ion involved in the initial oxygen sensing.

 

Option C. Chlorine: Chlorine ions do not play a significant role in the mechanism of peripheral oxygen sensing by chemoreceptors.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  •  Potassium ions are critical in the mechanism of peripheral oxygen sensing by chemoreceptors, where a decrease in oxygen levels leads to reduced potassium efflux, cell depolarization, and subsequent signaling to increase ventilation.

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old patient is being evaluated for cardiac function, and their myocardial action potential is studied. Based on the marked point on the action potential curve provided, which statement is true regarding the mechanisms at this point?

options.label: B
options.text: Due to closure of Na+ and opening of slow K+ channel

options.label: C
options.text: Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels

options.label: D
options.text: Due to opening of Na+ and closure of fast K+ channels

questions.answerText: Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels

 

  • The marked point on the myocardial action potential curve corresponds to the plateau phase (Phase 2) of the cardiac action potential.
  • This phase is characterized by a balance between the inward flow of calcium ions through slow (L-type) calcium channels and the outward flow of potassium ions.
  • The slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels maintains the membrane potential in a depolarized state, which is crucial for the contraction of the heart muscle, ensuring a sustained contraction necessary for effective pumping action.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Due to Na+/K+ ATPase pump: The Na+/K+ ATPase pump is primarily involved in maintaining the resting membrane potential and ionic gradients by pumping Na+ out and K+ into the cell. It is not responsible for the plateau phase of the action potential.

 

Option B. Due to closure of Na+ and opening of slow K+ channel: While the closure of fast Na+ channels occurs at the end of the initial depolarization, the opening of slow K+ channels happens later, contributing to repolarization rather than the plateau phase.

 

Option D. Due to opening of Na+ and closure of fast K+ channels: The opening of fast Na+ channels leads to the rapid depolarization (Phase 0) of the action potential, not the plateau phase. The closure of fast K+ channels also occurs early in the action potential process, not during the plateau phase.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The plateau phase (Phase 2) of the myocardial action potential is maintained by the slow but prolonged opening of L-type calcium channels, which allows for a sustained depolarization essential for effective cardiac muscle contraction.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old patient presents with chronic respiratory symptoms including shortness of breath and a persistent cough. The patient's spirometry results are shown in the graph, with the abnormal curve representing their condition. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) COPD

 

  • The graph shows spirometry results, comparing normal lung function (blue curve) with a diseased state (red curve).
  • The characteristic feature in the diseased curve is a reduced FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in one second) and a decreased FEV1/FVC (forced vital capacity) ratio, which is typical of obstructive lung diseases such as Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD).
  • In COPD, there is airflow limitation due to airway obstruction, which makes it difficult to expel air rapidly, hence the reduced FEV1.

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sarcoidosis: This condition typically presents with a restrictive pattern on spirometry, characterized by a proportional reduction in both FEV1 and FVC, leading to a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio. The graph does not depict this pattern.

 

Option C. Pulmonary fibrosis: Pulmonary fibrosis also presents with a restrictive pattern on spirometry, where both FEV1 and FVC are reduced proportionally, maintaining a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio. This is not shown in the graph.

 

Option D. Bronchiectasis: This condition can present with an obstructive pattern similar to COPD, but it is not as common as COPD in producing the specific spirometric pattern shown. COPD is a more likely diagnosis given the typical presentation and spirometry results.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The characteristic spirometry finding in COPD is a reduced FEV1 and a decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, indicative of obstructive airway disease.
  •  This distinguishes it from restrictive lung diseases such as sarcoidosis and pulmonary fibrosis, where the FEV1/FVC ratio is usually normal or increased.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of congestive heart failure is admitted to the hospital for worsening dyspnea and lower extremity edema. The physician suspects significant fluid retention and orders a test involving the administration of I-125 labelled albumin to measure his body fluid compartments accurately. Which of the following body fluid compartments is being measured with this technique?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Plasma volume

 

  • Iodine-125 (I-125) labeled albumin is specifically used to measure plasma volume.
  • Albumin, being a large protein, is confined to the intravascular space and does not cross into the interstitial or intracellular compartments.
  • When tagged with the radioactive isotope I-125, albumin allows for precise measurement of plasma volume by detecting the distribution of the isotope within the blood.
  • This measurement is particularly useful in clinical scenarios like congestive heart failure, where fluid status needs careful assessment.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Interstitial fluid volume: This refers to the fluid between cells within the extracellular space, which is not measured by I-125 labeled albumin since albumin remains in the plasma.

 

Option B. Intracellular fluid (ICF): The intracellular fluid is inside cells, and albumin cannot penetrate cell membranes to enter this compartment, so I-125 labeled albumin does not measure ICF.

 

Option C. Extracellular fluid (ECF): The ECF includes both plasma and interstitial fluid. However, I-125 labeled albumin is specifically used to measure the plasma portion, not the entire ECF.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • I-125 labeled albumin is used to measure plasma volume accurately because albumin stays within the intravascular compartment, making it ideal for assessing the plasma component of the extracellular fluid.


ul assessment.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with hirsutism, acne, and irregular menstrual cycles. Laboratory testing reveals elevated levels of androgens. The endocrinologist is trying to determine the source of excess androgen production. Which of the following hormones is exclusively secreted by the adrenal glands and not by the ovaries?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) DHEA-S

 

  • Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S) is a hormone that is exclusively produced by the adrenal glands.
  • It is a sulfated form of DHEA, which increases its solubility and half-life in the circulation.
  • DHEA-S is often used as a marker of adrenal androgen production in conditions like adrenal hyperplasia or adrenal tumors, where androgen excess is suspected.
  • Unlike DHEA, which is produced by both the adrenal glands and the ovaries, DHEA-S is specific to the adrenal cortex and is not produced by the ovaries.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Progesterone: Progesterone is produced by both the ovaries and the adrenal glands. It plays a significant role in the menstrual cycle and pregnancy, and thus cannot be used to distinguish adrenal from ovarian hormone production.

 

Option C. Estrogen: Estrogen is primarily produced by the ovaries, but small amounts can also be synthesized by the adrenal glands, especially through the aromatization of adrenal androgens. Therefore, estrogen is not exclusively adrenal in origin.

 

Option D. DHEA: Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) is produced by both the adrenal glands and the ovaries. It is a precursor to androgens and estrogens, making it non-specific for adrenal production.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • DHEA-S is a hormone exclusively secreted by the adrenal glands and not by the ovaries, making it a specific marker for evaluating adrenal androgen production.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old pregnant woman at 39 weeks of gestation is undergoing continuous fetal monitoring during labor. The fetal heart rate monitor shows frequent accelerations, which are interpreted as a sign of fetal well-being. Which of the following factors primarily contributes to these increases in fetal heart rate during labor and delivery?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Carotid body chemoreceptors

 

  • Carotid body chemoreceptors are sensitive to changes in the levels of oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH in the blood.
  • During labor, transient reductions in oxygen levels (hypoxia) or changes in carbon dioxide levels can occur, which are detected by these chemoreceptors.
  • In response, the carotid body chemoreceptors trigger reflexes that modulate the fetal heart rate, leading to accelerations as part of the fetal compensatory mechanisms to ensure adequate oxygen delivery and maintain homeostasis.
  • This reflex response indicates an intact and responsive autonomic system, which is crucial for fetal well-being.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Aortic baroreceptors: These are primarily involved in detecting changes in blood pressure but do not play a central role in the modulation of fetal heart rate accelerations during labor.

 

Option B. ANP (Atrial Natriuretic Peptide): ANP is involved in the regulation of blood volume and pressure but does not have a direct effect on the modulation of fetal heart rate accelerations.

 

Option C. Autonomic brain stem regulation: While the autonomic brainstem plays a role in overall heart rate regulation, the specific trigger for fetal heart rate accelerations during labor is more directly tied to chemoreceptor activity in response to blood gas levels.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Carotid body chemoreceptors are primarily responsible for detecting changes in blood oxygen and carbon dioxide levels during labor, leading to fetal heart rate accelerations that indicate good fetal health and adaptive capacity.

questions.stem: Which of the following events in the muscle contraction process is primarily responsible for the detachment of myosin from actin filaments, allowing the muscle to relax?

options.label: B
options.text: Cessation of calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

options.label: C
options.text: Dissociation of ADP and Pi from the myosin head

options.label: D
options.text: Attachment of ATP to the myosin head

questions.answerText: Attachment of ATP to the myosin head
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Attachment of ATP to the myosin head

 

  • During muscle contraction, the attachment and detachment of myosin to and from actin are crucial for the sliding filament mechanism.
  • After the power stroke, where myosin pulls actin, the myosin head remains attached to the actin filament until a new ATP molecule binds to the myosin head.
  • The binding of ATP causes a conformational change in the myosin head, leading to the detachment of myosin from actin.
  • This is essential for the continuation of the contraction cycle, allowing the myosin to reset and attach to a new site on the actin filament for the next contraction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Conformational change in Troponin T: This occurs in response to calcium binding to troponin C, which then moves tropomyosin away from the actin binding sites, allowing myosin to attach to actin, but it does not cause the detachment of myosin from actin.

 

Option B. Cessation of calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum: The cessation of calcium release leads to muscle relaxation by allowing calcium to be re-sequestered in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which prevents further actin-myosin interaction, but this process does not directly cause myosin detachment from actin.

 

Option C. Dissociation of ADP and Pi from the myosin head: This event occurs during the power stroke, leading to the movement of the actin filament but does not cause the detachment of myosin from actin.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The attachment of ATP to the myosin head is critical for the detachment of myosin from actin during the muscle contraction cycle, enabling the muscle to relax and prepare for the next contraction.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) undergoes a pulmonary function test (PFT) as part of his routine evaluation. The results indicate that at a specific lung volume, the pressure measured at the upper airway is zero, which corresponds to no net airflow in or out of the lungs. At which of the following lung volumes or capacities does this phenomenon occur?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Functional residual capacity

 

  • Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the lung volume at the end of a normal exhalation when the elastic recoil forces of the lungs are balanced by the outward pull of the chest wall.
  • At FRC, the pressure in the airways equals atmospheric pressure (zero), meaning there is no driving force for air to move in or out of the lungs, and the airflow is at equilibrium.
  • This is the point where the lungs are at rest between breaths, and the pressure in the upper airways is zero.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Total lung capacity: Total lung capacity (TLC) is the maximum volume of air that the lungs can hold after a maximal inhalation. At this point, the intrapleural pressure is very negative, and the airway pressure is not zero.

 

Option B. Inspiratory capacity: Inspiratory capacity (IC) is the volume of air that can be inhaled after a normal exhalation, but it does not represent the equilibrium point where airway pressure is zero.

 

Option C. Residual volume: Residual volume (RV) is the amount of air remaining in the lungs after a maximal exhalation, and at this volume, the airway pressure is not zero.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the lung volume at which airway pressure reaches zero, meaning there is no net movement of air in or out of the lungs, reflecting the equilibrium between lung and chest wall forces.
